sentences: This is the seventh of The Ten Largest, a series the Swedish painter Hilma af Klint completed in about forty days in the autumn of 1907.
The series moves through four stages of life, childhood, youth, adulthood and old age, and this sheet belongs to adulthood.
It is painted in tempera on paper more than three metres tall, probably laid out on the studio floor because of its size.
Spirals, petals, rounded forms and lines that look like letters float on a lilac ground, yet the letters spell nothing you can read.
The shapes turn the rhythms of life, growth, union and the balance of masculine and feminine, into something you can see.
It came years before Kandinsky's first abstractions, but in 1932 af Klint asked that her work be kept from the public for a long time.
When the Guggenheim in New York gave her a retrospective in 2018, it became the most visited exhibition in the museum's history.
